title: Unequal Entry, Unequal Preparation: Rethinking Graduate Teacher Recruitment in Sri Lanka Through a Teacher Education Lens
content: Sri Lanka admits people to the teaching profession through two very different doors. Advanced Level (A/L) school leavers enter National Colleges of Education (NCOEs) on the basis of district Z-scores, receive three years of residential pre-service training, and are then appointed to schools as a cohort. University graduates, by contrast, must compete in an open competitive examination built around an aptitude paper and a general knowledge paper, followed by an interview and a practical teaching test, and many of those who succeed enter classrooms with no pedagogical preparation at all. This article uses a critical policy analysis of recruitment gazettes, Ministry of Education notices, National Education Commission policy documents and World Bank and Institute of Policy Studies reviews to examine the fairness, validity and educational logic of this dual system. Drawing on research on teacher selection, organizational justice and teacher preparation, the article argues that the graduate examination is weakly aligned with the knowledge and dispositions that predict effective teaching, that it treats two groups of future teachers unequally at the point of entry, and that it moves the problem of preparation from before appointment to after it. The article proposes an alternative model in which graduates who intend to teach are identified early, selected on teaching-relevant criteria, and given structured pre-service training before appointment. The analysis contributes to debates on teacher recruitment in South Asia and offers concrete policy directions for Sri Lanka's ongoing education reform.
